name: The Nirvana Fallacy
statement: The nirvana fallacy rejects a workable solution by comparing it only to an idealized, unrealistic alternative rather than the real options.
statementAccent: comparing it only to an idealized, unrealistic alternative
meaning: The nirvana fallacy is the informal fallacy of judging real, imperfect solutions against a perfect, unattainable standard rather than against the realistic alternatives actually on offer. Because the imperfect solution will always look bad next to an idealised "nirvana," this framing can be used to reject genuinely beneficial policies or fixes.
mechanism: The fallacy sets up a false dichotomy between "flawed reality" and "flawless fantasy," so any shortcoming in the real proposal becomes grounds for dismissal, even when it is a clear improvement over the status quo. Demsetz’s alternative was the "comparative institution approach": judge options against each other, not against an ideal that isn’t available.

examples.text: In the 1980s, some critics opposed mandatory seatbelt laws by pointing out that belt-wearers still sometimes die in crashes, using the imperfection to argue against a measure that substantially reduces fatality risk.
Opposition to anti-drunk-driving campaigns on the grounds that some people will keep drinking and driving ignores that such campaigns still reduce the overall incidence.
Dismissing animal testing as worthless because thalidomide passed animal tests yet still caused harm treats one imperfect outcome as proof the entire practice provides no value.

whyItMatters: It matters in policy debate because it can block incremental, evidence-based improvements by demanding an unattainable standard of perfection, when the real choice is always between competing imperfect options rather than between imperfection and perfection.
limits: Pointing out that a proposal is significantly worse than a genuinely achievable alternative is not the nirvana fallacy — it applies only when the comparison point is unrealistic or unattainable, not when a better real option actually exists.
misreadings: The fallacy is often confused with simply criticising a solution’s shortcomings; legitimate critique of feasible alternatives is not nirvana-fallacious, only comparison against an idealised impossibility is.
origin: Economist Harold Demsetz introduced the "nirvana approach" as a target of criticism in his 1969 article "Information and Efficiency: Another Viewpoint," contrasting it with his "comparative institution approach"; Voltaire’s "the best is the enemy of the good" anticipated the idea.

sources.text: Nirvana fallacy, Wikipedia. — Demsetz’s 1969 "nirvana approach," the comparative-institution alternative, and the seatbelt, drunk-driving, and animal-testing examples.
"Harold Demsetz," The Concise Encyclopedia of Economics (Econlib). — his authorship and standing behind the nirvana-approach critique.
